query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal-oxidation treatment applied to conventional HEA surfaces induces a self-adaptive, nanoscale glaze oxide layer that simultaneously reduces both the friction coefficient and wear rate across a broad range of service temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional high-entropy alloy (HEA) used in self-lubricating moving components, which currently suffers from relatively high friction and accelerated wear under variable temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal-oxidation treatment (e.g., precise annealing or thermal shock) to promote in situ formation of a dense, nanostructured oxide glaze layer on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: The treatment-induced glaze layer should retain its integrity and lubricious properties over a wide service-temperature range (from room temperature up to near 800 °C) and under variable sliding loads reflective of real-world operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The self-adaptive nanoscale oxide glaze layer with a nanohierarchical architecture.
generation.mechanism: The thermal-oxidation treatment forms a stable oxide layer that adjusts its microstructure with temperature changes. At lower temperatures, the layer provides low shear resistance, while at high temperatures it densifies to resist adhesive and oxidative wear, thereby reducing both friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the treated alloy will exhibit a significantly lower friction coefficient and a decreased wear rate across the entire temperature range, with reductions observable in friction measurements and wear volume assessments.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (friction coefficient and wear rate) measured on the untreated HEA under identical testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only if the thermal-oxidation treatment is precisely controlled to avoid forming overly thick or brittle oxide layers that could spall, and if the operating conditions do not exceed the temperature or load limits where the glaze layer remains stable.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement and long-term stability of the glaze layer under extreme cyclic or impact conditions remain uncertain, as does its durability in environments with differing reactive species.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set to undergo the controlled thermal-oxidation treatment and a control set left untreated. Subject both sets to sliding wear tests across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under identical loads and sliding speeds. Use scanning electron microscopy and surface profilometry to characterize the oxide glaze layer, and measure friction coefficients and wear rates over extended cycles.
measurements: Coefficient of friction over time at different temperatures
Wear volume (mm³/N-m) using profilometry and mass loss analysis
Microstructural characterization (SEM, TEM) of the treated surface to confirm the formation and stability of the glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal-oxidation treated samples do not consistently show a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the untreated controls across the full temperature range, or if the glaze layer deteriorates or spalls under the operational conditions, then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

Inspired by the high-entropy effects, we replace minor alloying elements in nickel-based alloys with multicomponent alloying elements, which not only deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in the system but also enhance the ability of the system to generate glaze layers. This cooperative heterostructure can trigger gradient recrystallized tribo-layer through plastic deformation co-mediated by dislocation, SFs, and deformation twins (DT) during sliding at RT, thus accommodating elastic–plastic deformation and virtually eliminating wear. The intrinsic composition undulations can stabilize the friction interface and act twofold, not only by circumventing strain localization in the NC tribo-layer but also by densifying the glaze layer. We realize the above strategy in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 (at.%) CCA and reveal the origin of the nanohierarchical architecture by comparing it with its counterpart Ni75(AlNbTiV)25 CCA with lower alloying concentration (hereinafter named NiX and Ni3X, respectively). The wear mechanisms addressed in this work provide guidance for the fabrication of ultra-wear-resistant alloys by exploiting the multicomponent heterostructure

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

Additionally, the generated oxide layer covers the wear surface, effectively isolating contact between the coating and the friction counterpart, providing protection. Therefore, in addition to the adhesive and abrasive wear analyzed above, the wear mechanism of the coating also includes oxidative wear.

decision.trend: Early work on HEAs (PMC7515071) focused on achieving dense microstructures through rapid consolidation processes (e.g., spark plasma sintering) that exploited in situ formation of protective oxide layers to enhance wear resistance at higher temperatures. Subsequent studies (PMC10241162) introduced nanohierarchical architectures with composition undulation, resulting in adaptive friction interfaces that lowered wear rates over a moderate temperature span. More recent efforts (PMC10456374) have taken advantage of controlled thermal treatments (thermal shock/annealing) to induce dense composite oxide films on HEA films, which improved both oxidation resistance and tribocorrosion behavior under severe conditions. Overall, while these approaches individually improved friction or wear over specific temperature ranges, none have provided an integrated, unified solution effective across the extreme variability of service conditions.
decision.unsolved: The open challenge is to devise a single intervention that simultaneously reduces the coefficient of friction and the wear rate across a wide service-temperature range, thereby integrating both lubricity and robust wear resistance in one step.
decision.lever: controlled thermal-oxidation treatment to induce the formation of a self-adaptive, nanoscale glaze layer
decision.why: Building on the trend where adaptive surface layers (e.g., oxide films) have been shown to either reduce friction or enhance wear resistance at certain temperatures, a controlled oxidation treatment can be tuned to form a stable, nanostructured lubricious glaze. This layer can dynamically adjust its chemistry and structure with temperature variations, addressing both friction and wear performance across the full spectrum of operating conditions as required for self‐lubricating HEA moving components.

families.principle: Modifying the surface or interfacial properties (for instance, by applying a tailored coating) allows one to decouple the bulk alloy properties from the tribological response, achieving simultaneous friction reduction and wear resistance.
cues_for: self-lubricating moving components require an integrated surface feature
the untreated alloy’s lack of an integrated feature points to the potential of surface modifications
a single, engineered surface intervention has the potential to function across a wide range of service temperatures
cues_against: no explicit cues against this approach were mentioned, though one must ensure coating stability under variable temperatures
families.best_lever: Apply an adaptive, gradient surface coating (such as a multi-layer tribo-film based on MoS2/graphene composites) that chemically bonds to the HEA, maintains low friction and high wear resistance across the full temperature range, and whose performance can be directly assessed via wear testing.

families.principle: Altering the alloy’s elemental makeup can promote the formation of intrinsic, lubricious phases or solid lubricant precipitates that lower friction and enhance wear resistance.
cues_for: reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate
the untreated HEA lacks an integrated feature
cues_against: wide service-temperature range (risk that lubricious phases may degrade or transform at high or low temperatures)
families.best_lever: Introduce a dopant element (e.g., a minor addition of sulfur- or carbon-affinitive elements) engineered to form in situ lubricious precipitates that are thermodynamically stable across the target temperature spectrum.

families.principle: Modifying the synthesis method (e.g., rapid solidification or controlled cooling) can affect phase formation and distribution, potentially yielding self-lubricating microstructures.
cues_for: prior material modifications have separately targeted friction reduction
the conventional processing leaves the HEA lacking an integrated self-lubricating feature
cues_against: the need for a singular intervention that works over a wide temperature range might be difficult to achieve purely by processing adjustments
families.best_lever: Adopt a rapid solidification synthesis route designed to suppress coarse segregation and promote a uniform, metastable phase distribution that evolves into a lubricious phase under service conditions.

families.principle: Designing and controlling the internal microstructural architecture (e.g., engineered grain boundaries or phase distributions) can impart synergistic improvements in friction reduction and wear resistance.
cues_for: the untreated HEA lacks an integrated feature, suggesting that a designed microstructural architecture might provide combined functionality
prior attempts have separately targeted microstructural tuning
cues_against: achieving a unified solution across a wide service-temperature range remains challenging if relying solely on microstructural adjustments
families.best_lever: Engineer a microstructure with a tailored dispersion of low-shear-strength phases situated at grain boundaries to facilitate self-lubricating behavior while impeding wear, ensuring stability across temperatures.

families.principle: Controlled heat or thermomechanical treatments can trigger phase transformations or refine microstructures (e.g., fine precipitate formation) that improve both friction and wear performance.
cues_for: the need to perform under variable operating temperatures hints at the importance of thermally activated mechanisms
cues_against: prior attempts with separate friction or wear improvements indicate that simple annealing or thermomechanical treatments may be insufficient for integrated performance
such transient or heat-activated mechanisms may be hard to control uniformly across a wide temperature range
families.best_lever: Implement an optimized annealing protocol that induces the formation of a stable, fine dispersion of lubricious phases without compromising the alloy’s wear resistance at both low and high temperatures.
